result.summary: The Greeks plunder Troy, enslave its women and feast in triumph. Achilles' ghost demands Polyxeina's sacrifice, and after it the fleet sails, but Athena, with Zeus's weapons and Poseidon's help, wrecks it near Euboea for the outrage against Cassandra. Aias is killed, Nauplius lures ships onto rocks, and Poseidon floods away the Greek wall at Troy.

scenes.title: The sack ends; captives led away
scenes.summary: The Argives carry off treasure and Trojan women to the ships. Helen walks ashamed, yet all the Greeks gaze on her with wonder.
scenes.stakes: Helen fears the Achaeans may mishandle her; the captive women face slavery.

scenes.title: Mourning rivers; Greek victory feast
scenes.summary: Xanthus and the rivers mourn while the Greeks sacrifice, praise Sinon and hear a harper sing the war's story.

scenes.title: Helen and Menelaus reconciled
scenes.summary: In his tent Helen begs pardon and Menelaus forgives her, and they embrace.
scenes.stakes: Helen risks her husband's lasting anger.

scenes.title: Achilles' ghost demands Polyxeina
scenes.summary: Achilles' shade counsels his son and demands Polyxeina's sacrifice, threatening storms. At dawn the son tells the host.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks risk being storm-bound unless the sacrifice is made.

scenes.title: Polyxeina sacrificed; Hecuba transformed
scenes.summary: A storm confirms the demand. Polyxeina is slain at the tomb and buried by Antenor, the sea calms, and Hecuba is changed to a hound and then stone.
scenes.stakes: Polyxeina loses her life; Hecuba her child and form.

scenes.title: Departure across the Aegean
scenes.summary: The fleet sails past Tenedos and Lesbos while captives mourn and Cassandra laughs; Calchas warns in vain.
scenes.stakes: The Greeks sail heedless of Calchas' warning of destruction.

scenes.title: Athena arms for vengeance
scenes.summary: Athena complains of Aias' outrage against Cassandra; Zeus gives her his weapons, and she sends Iris to Aeolus.
scenes.stakes: Athena's honour demands vengeance; the Greek fleet is her target.

scenes.title: Storm and death of Aias
scenes.summary: Aeolus looses the winds and the fleet is shattered off Euboea. Aias survives defiantly until Poseidon buries him under a rock.
scenes.stakes: Aias and the fleet face drowning.

scenes.title: Wreck, false beacon, flooded wall
scenes.summary: Many perish; Nauplius lures ships with a false torch. Poseidon and Apollo then flood Troy's Greek wall, and survivors go home.
scenes.stakes: Odysseus is fated to suffer; Greek ships and men face destruction.

analysis.text: Victory turns to suffering: the sack's cruelty, the sacrifice of Polyxeina and the divine storm show that conquerors are punished for impiety.
The poem follows Quintus of Smyrna, a later Greek epic writer, who gathers earlier myth traditions of the Greek homecomings.

legacy.text: Polyxena's sacrifice and Hecuba's fate were treated by Euripides in his tragedy Hecuba.
Aias' punishment for violating Cassandra became a standard story of divine retribution in Greek art and the returns epics.

fun_facts.text: The Fall of Troy is by Quintus of Smyrna, probably written in the 3rd or 4th century AD, and continues Homer's Iliad.

language_notes.text: This is a heading summarizing the book's contents: the Greek victors' fleet will be destroyed by storm on the voyage home.
Danaans: another name for the Greeks (Argives, Achaeans), from the ancestor Danaus.
Haled means dragged or hauled by force.
Besprent means sprinkled or strewn over; the ashes are a sign of mourning.
'Thraldom's day that trapped her vainly loth' means the day of slavery that caught her, unwilling and resisting in vain.
Refers to the tale of Aphrodite (Queen of Love) caught with Ares in a net made by her husband Hephaestus, as the gods looked on.
Cytherea is Aphrodite, named for the island Cythera. Zeus is Helen's father in myth, which is why Helen is called his daughter.
"Burg" means a fortified town or city; here it is Troy. Xanthus is the Trojan river, personified as a god.
Epeius built the Wooden Horse that let the Greeks take Troy, so his work is "ever renowned."
"Cronos' Son" is Zeus. Even he cannot stop Destiny, though the text also says Zeus sanctions her deeds.
"Horse of Tree" means the wooden horse; "ambushed" refers to the warriors hidden inside it.
Sinon pretended to be a Greek deserter, endured Trojan torment, and persuaded them to haul the Horse inside the walls.
"Guerdons" are rewards; "misfeaturing" means his disfigurement, since the Trojans mutilated him.
"Goodlihead" is an archaic word for beauty or goodliness of appearance.
Lists episodes of the war: the gathering at Aulis, Achilles' raids, his fights with Telephus, Eetion and Cycnus, and the deaths of Hector, Penthesileia and Memnon (Tithonus' son).
"The child of Aeacus' son" is Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, whose father Peleus was son of Aeacus; he killed Eurypylus.
The Cyprian Queen is Aphrodite, goddess of love, so called from her cult on Cyprus; here she rekindles the couple's old affection.
"Wroth" is an archaic word meaning angry.
Alexander is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince who took Helen from Sparta.
"Death-noose" means hanging; "essay" means attempt; "comfortable words" are comforting words, and "salve" means soothe.
The "sweet child" is Hermione, Helen's daughter, whom she left behind in Sparta.
"Made sweet moan" means wept and murmured tenderly together; "spousal" means of marriage.
"Shade" means ghost or spirit of the dead; "bane" means destroyer, the thing that brings ruin.
"Vex not thine heart" is archaic: do not trouble or torment your heart. "Thine" and "thy" are old forms of "your."
Briseis was the captive woman Agamemnon took from Achilles in the Iliad, causing Achilles' great wrath and withdrawal from battle.
"Portion of the spoil" refers to the prize of war: captives were divided among the Greek leaders.
The Elysian Plain is the Greek paradise where favoured dead dwell. Here it is linked to heaven by a path.
"Child of Mist" is a poetic name for Dawn (Eos), who rises scattering night.
"Hest" means command; "guerdon" means reward or prize.
Achilles' father Peleus was mortal, but his mother Thetis was a sea goddess; the Greeks here call him Zeus's seed because Zeus was his great-grandfather (via Aeacus).
"Maid" means a young unmarried girl, here Polyxeina, Priam's daughter.
Hymen was the god of weddings; his hymn was the marriage song. Polyxeina was to be a bride, but is sacrificed instead.
Antenor was a Trojan elder who had favored peace with the Greeks, so he was spared when Troy fell.
Pallas the Unwearied One is Athena, here under her title Pallas; "unwearied" is a stock epithet.
Neleus' son is Nestor, the aged Greek counsellor from Pylos.
Earth-shaker is Poseidon's epithet, since he was god of earthquakes as well as the sea.
"Or ever unto Troy they came" means "before they ever came to Troy"; "therewithal" means "in addition to that."
"Had fain withheld" means he would gladly have held back; "fain" means willingly or gladly.
The Rocks Capherean are the cliffs of Euboea, where much of the Greek fleet was wrecked on the voyage home.
Calchas and Amphilochus were said to travel overland to Asia Minor, to Pamphylia and Cilicia, instead of sailing with the fleet.
Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles, between Asia Minor and Europe.
"Unbraided hair" and scored breasts are conventional signs of mourning in ancient Greek epic.
Cassandra, Priam's daughter, was cursed by Apollo to prophesy truly but never be believed, so her warnings of doom were ignored.
Dardania-land is the Trojan territory, named for Dardanus, an ancestor of the Trojans; "hoised" means hoisted.
Sminthian Phoebus is Apollo worshipped at Chrysa as "Sminthian", a cult title linked with mice; Cilla also had his shrine.
"Reck not of thee" means "pay no heed to you"; "forasmuch as" means "since" or "because".
Aias son of Oileus (the Locrian) dragged Cassandra from Athena's statue, where she had taken refuge, during the sack of Troy.
The Cyclops forged Zeus's thunderbolts, a reward for his freeing them, according to tradition.
Aegis: Athena's awe-inspiring goat-skin shield or breastplate; "adamantine" means unbreakable, and "massy" means massive.
Caphereus is the rocky Euboean headland where the Greek fleet is destined to be wrecked.
"Buffering" means battering; "madding" means maddening or raging.
"Thou hadst said" means "you would have said", addressing the reader directly.
Inverted word order: 'Him found she' means 'she found him'. The 'she' is Athena, who has come to Aeolus, keeper of the winds.
Trident is Poseidon's three-pronged spear, his emblem as god of the sea and earthquakes.
'Palling' means dimming or darkening; the mist veils the ships like a funeral pall.
'His brother's glorious child' is Athena, daughter of Zeus, who is Poseidon's brother. Poseidon helps her revenge against the Achaeans.
Atrytone ('the unwearied') is an epithet of Athena; 'welkin' is an old word for the sky.
The captive maids are Trojan women taken by the Greeks. 'Foul outrage' refers to their enslavement and mistreatment.
Trito-born is another epithet of Athena, from a name linked to her birth, tied to the Tritonis water.
The Titans were an older race of giant gods who fought Zeus and the Olympians.
'Shaker of Earth' is Poseidon's epithet, for his power over earthquakes.
Myth says Athena crushed the giant Enceladus beneath Sicily. His breath was said to cause the fires of Mount Etna.
"Drave" is an archaic past tense of "drive"; ships plunged forward, prows driven under the waves.
Deucalion's deluge: in Greek myth Zeus flooded the world; Deucalion and his wife survived in a chest, like the Greek Noah story.
"Too strait for them" means too narrow; the beaches could not hold all the corpses.
Nauplius' son Palamedes was killed through Greek treachery at Troy, so Nauplius seeks revenge by wrecking the fleet.
"Weird" means fate or destiny, not strangeness.
"Far-darter" is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god; "Shaker of Earth" is Poseidon.
Sigeum is a headland near Troy, on the Hellespont coast.

context_notes.text: Dawn, a goddess, rises each morning from the stream of Ocean encircling the world.
Menelaus is Helen's husband; her flight with Paris began the war.
Cassandra, Priam's prophetic daughter, goes to Agamemnon. Andromache, Hector's widow, goes to Achilles' son. Hecuba, Priam's queen, goes to Ulysses (Odysseus).
Xanthus, also called Scamander, was the river of Troy; the Nymphs are his attendant water spirits.
Simois was another Trojan river; Ida is the mountain near Troy.
Many Greeks suffered storms and disasters on their voyages home, which this line foreshadows.
Menelaus, king of Sparta, is Helen's husband. Her abduction by Paris caused the Trojan War, and Troy has now fallen.
Menelaus is called "wise of wit", a Homeric-style epithet; here his wisdom shows as willingness to forgive.
The speaker is Achilles' dead spirit, appearing to his son Neoptolemus, who came to Troy after Achilles' death.
Polyxeina (Polyxena) is a daughter of King Priam of Troy. Achilles was said to have loved her, and she is demanded as a sacrifice at his tomb.
Greek ships depended on fair seas; a god or spirit raising storms could keep the fleet from sailing home.
Dardans here are the Trojans, named for their ancestor Dardanus.
The speaker is Neoptolemus, Achilles' son. Achilles' ghost demanded Polyxeina's sacrifice before the Greeks could sail home.
Calchas was the Greek seer. The Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles.
Calchas was the Greek seer who had guided the army with his prophecies throughout the war.
Antenor was a Trojan elder, traditionally spared by the Greeks, who leads the survivors in burying the dead.
Athena (Minerva) was angered by the Greeks' impiety at Troy, notably Ajax's outrage against Cassandra, and she sent the storm against the fleet.
Euboea is a large island east of mainland Greece. The Greek ships are sailing home past it.
Medusa was a Gorgon whose head turned onlookers to stone; it was set on Athena's aegis.
Aeolus, son of Hippotas, is keeper of the winds, which he holds shut in caves on his island.
Caphereus is a dangerous rocky headland at the southeast of Euboea, where the Greek fleet was said to be wrecked.
Aias here is the Locrian Aias (the lesser), who assaulted Cassandra in Athena's temple, which provoked Athena's anger.
Aias is killed by the gods' hostility, punished for his impiety at Troy.
Nauplius is a son of Poseidon in myth, which is why he prays to his sea-god father.
Wreckers lit false lights on dangerous coasts to lure ships onto rocks; Nauplius uses this trick on the returning Greeks.
The Greek wall was built to protect the ships; Poseidon resented it, as it was raised without proper sacrifice to the gods.
The Euxine is the Black Sea; the Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles.

literary_notes.text: The Greeks pouring toward the ships are compared to mountain floods sweeping trees and rock, conveying overwhelming, destructive force.
The wailing captive women are likened to herded swine crying to one another, stressing their helplessness and loss of status.
Helen's blush is compared to Aphrodite's shame in Hephaestus' net, linking Helen's adultery with the goddess's exposure.
Gazing at Helen as at a goddess shows her beauty overriding blame.
The Greeks' relief at seeing Helen is likened to sailors sighting their homeland, showing how her beauty erases their suffering.
The river Xanthus mourns with his Nymphs as a grieving god, giving the landscape a share in Troy's fall.
Troy's ruin is compared to hail flattening ripe wheat, making the river's grief and the farmer's loss alike.
The Greeks' joyful shouting is likened to the clamour of jackdaws after a storm, suggesting relief after hardship.
This blunt line darkens the celebration by hinting at the Greeks' troubled homecomings.
The Greeks dream of peaceful days, while the reader knows many will meet disaster on the way home.
Aphrodite is pictured brooding over their souls like a bird over eggs, making divine influence explain their renewed love.
Forgetfulness becomes a dark mansion in which past griefs are locked away, picturing forgiveness as sealing up memories.
Fear "flitted" from her heart and hope "came", treating emotions as creatures that depart and arrive.
The couple's embrace is compared to vine and ivy intertwined, suggesting a bond no force can break.
Honour is imagined as a tall tree whose fruit only the strong and striving can climb to pluck.
Human life is compared to grass blossoms that fade as others bloom, stressing mortality and the call to kindness.
The threat of storms anticipates the troubled voyage and delay that will hold the Greeks if they ignore him.
Dawn is described as a figure who rises, scatters night and unveils the earth.
Polyxeina is compared to a calf dragged from its mother, stressing her innocence and helplessness as a sacrificial victim.
Tears are likened to oil pressed from olives under sacks and levers, conveying forced, heavy outpouring of grief.
Hecuba's dream of blood on Achilles' tomb anticipates the sacrifice that is about to happen.
Hecuba's wailing is compared to a bereaved dog whose pups were taken, prefiguring her later transformation into a hound.
A dead man's heart is warmed by living blood, a grim reversal of life and death.
Her blood-reddened body is compared to snow stained by a wounded animal, contrasting purity with violence.
Hecuba's change into stone ends her sorrow and makes her suffering a lasting marvel.
Fate is given a will of its own, as a malignant power that actively deludes men's minds.
The chiefs' prayers for safe return dissolve into the air, ironically signalling that the gods will not grant them.
The unknowing babies beside their grieving mothers deepen the pity of the scene.
Cassandra's laughter springs from anguish, so a sign of joy expresses bitter grief.
The sense that the shore keeps sliding away from the ships mirrors the soldiers' wistful, divided feelings.
"Loud hummed" and "crashed" imitate the sounds of wind and waves, making the voyage vivid.
Athena's complaint that evil goes unpunished and good men suffer questions the gods' justice, and her demand for vengeance answers it.
The clang of the aegis-links is compared to the sky crashing after lightning, conveying the goddess's terrifying power.
Clouds, night and haze gather as she arms, so nature itself darkens to match her wrath and foreshadows the storm.
Athena's quaking advance is likened to Zeus himself rushing to war, showing her as her father's equal in might.
Waves are compared to mountain-cliffs, conveying their enormous size and solidity.
Sea, sky and land seem fused into one, exaggerating the storm's chaos.
Comparing Aias to a Titan makes him a giant who defies the gods.
Affliction is described as wearing him down, making suffering a force with intent.
Aias's defiant boast shows his pride and impiety, the quality that brings his doom.
The myth of Enceladus makes Aias's burial parallel to a giant punished by a god.
The sky streaming "like a river" conveys the overwhelming volume of rain.
The sea "paved" with beams pictures the wreckage as a road, showing the scale of destruction.
The false torch promises safety but brings death; the "awful welcome" of the rocks mocks the sailors' hope.
Athena's fear for Odysseus anticipates his long, suffering journey home.
The beach and land "roared" and the headland "quaked," as if the earth itself cried out in the gods' violence.
